questions.subject: oral-reading
questions.spokenPassage: My grandmother woke us at midnight and told us to put our coats on over our pyjamas. Green light rippled across the whole northern sky, folding and unfolding like a curtain. Nobody said anything for a long time.

questions.subject: oral-reading
questions.spokenPassage: The trail to the lookout climbed steadily for two kilometres before it levelled off. I wanted to stop halfway, but my cousin promised the view was worth it. When we finally reached the top, I had to admit she was right.

questions.subject: oral-reading
questions.spokenPassage: In winter the river freezes hard enough to drive across, and crews mark a road on the ice with small spruce trees. Trucks carry fuel and supplies to communities that have no highway the rest of the year. The road exists for only a few weeks, and then the ice remembers it was a river.

questions.subject: oral-reading
questions.spokenPassage: Elijah McCoy designed a device that oiled train engines while they were still moving. Before his invention, engineers had to stop the train and oil the parts by hand, which wasted hours on every trip. Railways across the continent eventually adopted his design.

questions.subject: oral-reading
questions.spokenPassage: Our class turned the empty lot beside the school into a vegetable garden. We hauled soil in wheelbarrows and argued for a week about what to plant. By August the tomatoes had grown taller than most of the students who planted them.

questions.subject: oral-reading
questions.spokenPassage: Engineers build bridges to bend slightly rather than stand perfectly rigid. A structure that cannot move at all will crack when the temperature changes or the wind pushes against it. Flexibility, in this case, is not a weakness but the entire point.

questions.subject: oral-reading
questions.spokenPassage: Each autumn the Arctic tern leaves the Arctic and flies nearly to Antarctica, then turns around and does it again in spring. Over a lifetime, a single bird may travel far enough to reach the moon and return. Scientists still do not fully understand how it navigates.

questions.subject: oral-reading
questions.spokenPassage: The town archive occupies two rooms above the old post office, and almost nobody visits. Inside are newspapers, photographs and letters covering a hundred and forty years. The volunteer who runs it says the hardest part is deciding what is worth keeping.

questions.subject: oral-reading
questions.spokenPassage: Beneath much of the northern landscape lies permafrost, ground that has remained frozen for thousands of years. As temperatures rise, that ground begins to thaw, and buildings constructed on what was once solid footing start to tilt. Communities are now rebuilding infrastructure that was designed for a climate that no longer exists.

questions.subject: oral-reading
questions.spokenPassage: Translating a poem is not the same as translating a set of instructions. A translator must decide, line by line, whether to preserve the literal meaning or the rhythm, knowing that keeping both is usually impossible. The best translations are honest about what they chose to sacrifice.

questions.subject: oral-reading
questions.spokenPassage: On a remote Norwegian island, a vault buried in a mountainside stores seeds from nearly every food crop on earth. The facility exists so that agriculture could be rebuilt after a catastrophe, whether regional or global. It is, in effect, a backup copy of the world's food supply.

questions.subject: oral-reading
questions.spokenPassage: Economists use the phrase tragedy of the commons to describe a shared resource that everyone has an incentive to exploit and no one has an incentive to protect. A fishery, a pasture or an atmosphere can be depleted not through malice but through the accumulated weight of individually reasonable decisions. The difficulty is that solutions generally require collective agreement, which is precisely what the situation lacks.

questions.subject: oral-reading
questions.spokenPassage: Geologists read exposed rock faces the way a historian reads a manuscript, interpreting each layer as evidence of a particular interval of time. A band of ash marks a volcanic eruption; an abrupt change in sediment may record a coastline that advanced or retreated. What appears to be an unremarkable cliff is, to a trained eye, a detailed and largely reliable account.

questions.subject: oral-reading
questions.spokenPassage: Scientific consensus is frequently misunderstood as a vote, when it is closer to the residue left behind after decades of sustained attempts at refutation. An idea earns consensus not because researchers agree to accept it, but because repeated efforts to demonstrate that it is wrong have failed. That distinction matters enormously when the findings become inconvenient.
